summary:
The Archipiélago de San Andrés, Providencia y Santa Catalina is a department of Colombia and stands under the national framework: Colombia's formal legal framework is among the most developed in Latin America. Since a rule change approved in June 2015, trans Colombians change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments. The official Reyes, who defended the change, described those examinations as "profoundly invasive of privacy rights... rooted in unacceptable prejudice".

Constitutional Court jurisprudence dating from 1993 recognises legal gender recognition on the basis of self-recognition without a surgical requirement, and national identification documents have carried "trans" and "non-binary" markers since November 2025. A trans visitor therefore enters on identity documents that can be changed without medical evidence, and the marker itself is a recognised category rather than an irregularity.

Entry and partner recognition are settled in the visitor's favour. The first same-sex marriage conducted abroad was registered in Colombia in March 2016, and the National Registry issued a memo ordering all notaries and registrars to register same-sex marriages performed outside the country. Same-sex couples married abroad are entitled to the same visa, healthcare benefits, inheritance and pension rights as heterosexual spouses once they present a stamped marriage certificate and identification papers at the nearest designated office. Marriage equality has been available since 2016 and adoption by same-sex couples since 2015.

Access to commercial and public premises is protected by judgments T-314 of 2011 (Tequendama Hotel), T-909 of 2011 (Cosmocentro mall guards in Cali) and T-301 of 2004 (Santa Marta police at the city boardwalk). A 2011 Constitutional Court ruling allowed a transgender woman prisoner to choose her own hairstyle and makeup, and a Colombian court has since issued a ruling on the treatment of trans detainees.

The binding risk to a visitor is lethal anti-trans violence in the country as a whole. On 4 April 2025 Sara Millerey, a 32-year-old trans woman, was attacked in Bello, Antioquia; the assault was filmed and the video went viral on 5 April and she died that afternoon. Police interrogated local residents and no one had been arrested even after President Petro ordered an urgent investigation. EL PAÍS English reported on 14 April 2025 that 13 trans people had been killed by hate in Colombia in the first quarter of 2025, alongside earlier killings of gay men and the stabbing death of a trans rough-sleeper. The Attorney General's Office recorded 35 LGBTI murders between January and May 2025.

Some of the targeting is organised. The Guardian reported on 30 July 2024 that armed groups in Caquetá department ran a "social cleansing" campaign, distributing flyers on the street and via WhatsApp naming "faggots, lesbians and men and women who destroy homes" as legitimate military targets. Three armed men told a trans woman and local election candidate she had one week to leave town; she hid for a week, then fled at night. A second trans woman said a friend was killed. In Guajira, armed groups have posted flyers carrying a kill list of named individuals since March 2024, stating that "all will be military targets... homosexuals, lesbians, rapists, trans". Trans salon owner Tatiana Cespedes was forced to move twice after death threats from armed men.

Protection machinery exists but has not closed the gap. In July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, the state acknowledging conflict-driven violence as gender persecution, a crime against humanity; the UN Human Rights Committee noted concern. In May 2025 the UN Independent Expert on SOGI violence and discrimination, Graeme Reid, concluded a fact-finding mission across multiple Colombian cities, praising the government's legal reforms while warning of a stark disconnect between institutional progress and daily lived experience.

The Archipiélago de San Andrés, Providencia y Santa Catalina has no recorded incident, law or enforcement finding specific to trans visitors. What bears on a visitor to the islands is the national pattern of lethal anti-trans violence and the national legal guarantees described above.
tangentialFactors:
Colombia's recognition regime compares favourably with the rest of Latin America, but the country's record on killings sits at the opposite end of the regional scale: eight trans women were killed between February and April 2024 and 41 in 2023, and more than 40 transgender women were killed in 2023 according to national reporting. Killings of queer Colombians continued after the Millerey case, described in reporting as calculated brutality persisting amid the country's decades-long civil conflict.

Discrimination also shapes what trans women can do for a living. In Caquetá, discrimination limits trans women mainly to hairdressing or sex work, and trans women in the department have few options beyond sex work; that economic confinement is part of the exposure a visitor observes rather than a legal rule.

The armed-group campaigns in Guajira and Caquetá are department-level phenomena driven by non-state actors operating in conflict-affected territory. A visitor to the islands is not entering that theatre, but the national kill totals are compiled from the same period and the same country.

Sanctions and investigations have followed individual cases without producing arrests quickly: in the Millerey attack police questioned local residents and the president ordered an urgent investigation, yet no arrests had been made when EL PAÍS reported on 14 April 2025.
localsOnly:

National identification documents have carried "trans" and "non-binary" markers since November 2025.

Residents in same-sex relationships hold the full package of family rights: marriage equality since 2016 and adoption by same-sex couples since 2015, plus equal treatment of marriages performed abroad for visa, healthcare, inheritance and pension purposes once a stamped certificate and identification papers are presented.

A 2016 Ministry of Interior decree set procedural obligations for government institutions covering LGBTI rights in public education, health care, prisons and as victims of armed conflict, and a May 2018 executive decree by President Juan Manuel Santos extended guarantees to housing, work, recreation, sports and culture.

Detainees and prisoners have enforceable rights of their own: a 2011 Constitutional Court ruling allowed a transgender woman prisoner to choose her own hairstyle and makeup, and a Colombian court has since issued a ruling on the treatment of trans detainees. In July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, the state acknowledging conflict-driven violence as gender persecution, a crime against humanity.

Where armed-group flyers operate, the threat is named and personal. Since March 2024 groups in Guajira have circulated kill lists of identified individuals, and in Caquetá three armed men gave a trans local election candidate a week to leave before she fled at night; Tatiana Cespedes moved twice after death threats from armed men.
outOfScopeNotes:
The Archipiélago de San Andrés, Providencia y Santa Catalina has no recorded incident, law or enforcement finding specific to trans visitors in the available sources. Nothing in the inventory documents how the national notary route, the National Registry's marriage memo or the facility judgments are applied on the islands themselves; whether island notary and registry offices implement them without local variation is not sourced.

The sources describe the cause of Sara Millerey's death differently: one account has her drowning in a creek after being unable to swim with fractured limbs, another records cardiac arrest on the afternoon of 5 April 2025. The discrepancy is unresolved; the date of the attack, the filming, the viral spread of the video on 5 April and the absence of arrests after the president's order are consistent across accounts.

No source establishes a trans-specific offence, penalty or enforcement pattern inside the department, and no source quantifies police or prosecutorial response to anti-trans complaints on the islands. The hate-crime figures cited (13 trans people killed in the first quarter of 2025, 35 LGBTI murders between January and May 2025, 41 trans women killed in 2023, eight killed between February and April 2024) are national totals and are not broken down by department.

Whether the July 2023 indictment by the Special Jurisdiction for Peace, the 2016 Ministry of Interior decree or the May 2018 executive decree have produced measurable compliance in the Archipiélago is not sourced. Graeme Reid's May 2025 mission covered multiple Colombian cities; the inventory does not say whether the islands were visited.
